**The Weight of a Thousand Words**

I.

The first time I realized words had weight was when my father told me, *"You’re not trying hard enough."* I was eight, struggling with long division, my fingers smudged with pencil lead, my eraser reduced to pink dust. The words didn’t just land—they settled, like a stone dropped into a still pond. Ripples spread through me, and for years, I carried that stone in my chest, turning it over whenever I failed at something new.

Words are not just sounds. They are architecture. They build cathedrals in our minds or brick us into cells. A lover’s *"I don’t think we should see each other anymore"* can collapse a future you’d already started living in. A stranger’s *"You look tired"* can make you examine your face in every reflective surface for weeks. We are made and unmade by syllables.

II.

I once knew a woman who collected compliments like rare coins. She kept a small notebook in her purse, and whenever someone said something kind—*"Your laugh is infectious," "You have such a way with words," "I feel safe with you"*—she’d write it down, date it, and tuck it away. On bad days, she’d read them aloud to herself in the bathroom mirror. *"You are enough,"* she’d whisper, borrowing the words of others because her own had failed her.

I asked her once if it worked.
*"Sometimes,"* she said. *"But only if I believe the person who said it."*

That’s the catch, isn’t it? Words are only as heavy as the hands that deliver them.

III.

There’s a myth—maybe it’s true—that the ancient Egyptians weighed the heart against a feather to judge the soul’s worth. I like to imagine words work the same way. Some are feathers: *"Good morning," "I like your shirt," "The coffee’s ready."* They lift, briefly, before drifting away. Others are anvil-heavy: *"I never loved you," "You’ll amount to nothing," "This is your fault."* They don’t just weigh on the heart; they crack it.

I wonder what would happen if we treated words like physical objects. If *"I’m sorry"* was a bandage you had to press onto a wound, would we say it more carefully? If *"You’re beautiful"* was a seed you planted in someone’s palm, would we mean it when we spoke?

IV.

The heaviest word I know is *"why."*

It’s the word of children and philosophers, the word that follows tragedy like a shadow. *"Why her?" "Why now?" "Why me?"* It’s a word that demands an answer the universe rarely provides. It’s the word that turns grief into a labyrinth.

My mother asked it when my brother didn’t come home. The police used softer words—*"accident," "sudden," "peaceful"*—but none of them could hold the weight of her *"why."* It sat between us at the kitchen table, a silent third guest, long after the casseroles stopped arriving.

V.

I read once that the average person speaks about 16,000 words a day. That’s 16,000 opportunities to build or destroy, to heal or wound, to lie or tell the truth. Most of them are forgettable—*"Pass the salt," "What time is it?" "See you tomorrow."* But some linger. Some become part of the furniture of a life.

I think about the words I’ve wasted. The *"I’m fines"* when I wasn’t. The *"It’s not a big deal"* when it was. The *"I love yous"* said out of habit, not feeling. Words can be currency, and I’ve been careless with mine.

VI.

There’s a game I play sometimes when I’m alone in public places—coffee shops, park benches, subway cars. I listen to snippets of conversation and invent backstories.

*"You can’t just—"*
(A marriage dissolving over cold coffee.)

*"But what if I fail?"*
(A student on the verge of dropping out.)

*"I should’ve told you sooner."*
(A secret kept too long.)

It’s astonishing how much weight a half-heard sentence can carry. How much life is lived in the spaces between words.

VII.

The lightest word I know is *"maybe."*

It’s the word of possibility, of doors left ajar. *"Maybe next year."* *"Maybe things will change."* *"Maybe I was wrong."* It’s a word that doesn’t commit, doesn’t promise, doesn’t break. It floats, untethered, and that’s both its gift and its curse.

I’ve lived in the land of *"maybe"* for years. *"Maybe I’ll write that book."* *"Maybe I’ll leave this job."* *"Maybe I’ll be happy."* It’s a comfortable place, soft around the edges, but it’s also where dreams go to hibernate.

VIII.

I once wrote a letter I never sent. It was to an old friend, someone I’d hurt with careless words years ago. I filled three pages with apologies, explanations, memories. I folded it into an envelope, addressed it, even bought a stamp. But I couldn’t bring myself to drop it in the mailbox.

Words on a page are permanent in a way spoken words aren’t. They can be reread, dissected, held against you. I wasn’t brave enough to let mine exist in the world.

I still have the letter. It’s in a shoebox under my bed, next to a postcard from my grandfather and a napkin with a phone number I never called.

IX.

What if we had to carry the words we spoke? Not just remember them, but *feel* their weight. *"You’re ugly"* would be a boulder. *"I forgive you"* would be a feather made of lead. *"I don’t know"* would be a backpack full of question marks.

Would we speak less? Would we mean more?

X.

I have 100 words left, and I’m thinking about silence. About how sometimes the absence of words is the heaviest thing of all. The things we don’t say—the *"I’m scared," "I need help," "I miss you"*—they don’t disappear. They sit in our throats, our chests, our stomachs, growing heavier with each unspoken day.

XI.

Fifty words now. I’m thinking about the word *"home."* How it can mean a place, a person, a feeling. How it can be a sanctuary or a cage. How some people spend their whole lives searching for it, and others never realize they’ve had it all along.

XII.

Twenty words. I’m thinking about you, reading this. About the words you carry. About the ones you wish you could take back, the ones you wish you’d said. About how we’re all just trying to balance the weight.

XIII.

Ten.

Nine.

Eight.

Seven.

Six.

Five.

Four.

Three.

Two.

One.

*(Breathe.)*
